# Images and surface maps

::: {.doc-lead}
Show calibrated images, channels and projected mesh data alongside ordinary plots.
:::

## Images and scale bars

These patterns assume `import numpy as np`, `import fluxplot as fp`, an axes `ax`, and image
arrays (`dapi`, `gfp`) from your analysis.

```python
im = fp.image(
    ax, np.stack([dapi, gfp]), series="cells", channels=["dapi", "gfp"],
    luts=["blue", "green"],
    display_range=[(0, 900), None],   # None: the 1st–99.8th percentiles
    pixel_size=0.325, units="µm",
    composite="add",                  # or "max"
)
fp.scalebar(ax, 10, "µm")             # a vector bar exactly 10 data units long
fp.colorbar(im.mappables["gfp"], ax=ax, name="gfp", label="GFP")
```

`fp.image` takes a `(H, W)` image or a `(C, H, W)` / `(H, W, C)` stack. It gives every channel a
LUT (a colormap name, or a colour, meaning a black-to-colour ramp) and a display range (the
black and white points), composites the channels into one RGB `imshow` in Python, and puts the
axes in physical units from `pixel_size`.

Each channel is a colour scale in the manifest (`cells.dapi`, `cells.gfp`; for a single 2D
image, just `cells`) with a linear norm over its display range, and a recipe control of the same
name. Flux's colour-scale editor therefore adjusts a channel's brightness, contrast or LUT and
reruns the script. The scale is marked `recolor: "regenerate"`, or `"raster"` when you pass
`value_raster=True` so that the channel's values are saved beside the SVG. The series' `image`
payload records the channels, LUTs, display ranges, pixel size, units, extent and composite.

`fp.scalebar` draws a `Line2D` exactly `length` data units long, anchored in a corner (`loc`) and
drawn in the theme's ink. Its label (`"<length> <units>"`) is the part `scalebar.<n>.label`. The
fluxplot repository's `examples/image_example.py` draws a complete two-channel field.

## Surface maps

```python
# lh_vertices, lh_faces, ... and the per-vertex labels come from your analysis.
fp.surface(ax, labels, series="blocks",
           surfaces={"left": (lh_vertices, lh_faces),
                     "right": (rh_vertices, rh_faces)},
           kind="label", legend=True)
```

`surfaces` maps each hemisphere to a `(vertices, faces)` pair or a GIFTI file path (read with
`nibabel`, an optional dependency). The second argument, `values` (here `labels`), holds one
value per vertex. `kind` is `"label"`,
`"continuous"`, or `"auto"` (the default, which chooses label maps for integral, few-valued
data); see [`fp.surface`](/docs/fluxplot-api.html#surface) for every option.

A label map draws **one collection per category**, so every region becomes a separately
addressable, separately recolourable part (`blocks.<category>`; the group `blocks.regions`
lists them all) with a matching legend key. A
continuous map draws one field (`blocks.field`) plus a colorbar. The manifest records the
complete value-to-colour contract: `cmap`, `color_range`, the category-to-colour table, and which
vertices were treated as missing. Views (`lateral`, `medial`, …) and hemispheres are laid out
side by side inside the one axes.

Vertices with no data are an explicit `missing` part rather than a value, so an on-mesh zero stays
distinguishable from absent data and sentinel codes grey out instead of becoming a spurious category.
Rendering is orthographic with back-face culling — a fold cannot paint over the surface in front of
it — with optional Lambertian `shading` for relief; a face straddling a boundary takes the majority
label rather than being dropped.

For an orbitable mesh rather than a projected view, use [3D plots](/docs/3d-plots.html).
